entries.title: CRC-32 on PCLMULQDQ and the ARMv8 CRC32 instructions
entries.body:
Crc32.update in native x86-64 and AArch64 builds now runs a hardware kernel when the CPU has one, and the Nish table walk everywhere else, with bit-identical results. x86-64 folds with PCLMULQDQ and finishes with a Barrett reduction; AArch64 uses the ARMv8 CRC32 instructions (a PMULL fold measured 17-22% slower and was dropped). The path is chosen once per process in the new runtime/runtime-checksum.c, with per-function target attributes and no -march; NISH_CRC32=soft forces the tables. Targets without a kernel (i686, armv7, wasm, Node) keep the walk.

Measured: 7.6-9.2x on 4 KiB-1 MiB on x86-64 (band 2-7%), 6.3-7.5x on AArch64 (band under 1%); gzip decompress 1.11-1.12x
Refs: docs/wp38-simd.md, docs/security/compress.md (COMP-13)
Tests: tests/simd/crc32.c, tests/link/std_compress_crc_paths, tests/link/std_compress_crc_diff, tests/link/std_compress_gzip_files

Part of #1059

entries.title: record each value's source range in JsonDocument with parseRanged
entries.body:
JsonDocument.parseRanged and parseTextRanged parse as parse and parseText do, and also record the byte range of every value and of every member key, so a schema validator can point a diagnostic at the bytes a value came from. start, end, keyStart and keyEnd read the ranges (-1 where none was recorded), and setRange and setKeyRange give built values one, for a loader that builds a document from another format.

A plain parse costs nothing for this. Ranges are stamped with the generation they were written in, so parse writes and resets nothing, and clear changes only on the one step in 511 that wraps the generation. The range arrays live in a holder made on first use, so a document that never keeps ranges never allocates them. parseRanged has its own copies of the hot helpers, so the originals still inline into parse.
metrics: retired instructions against main (cachegrind, copy band 0.000%): plain parse -25/-17/-19/-11,723 on twitter/citm/canada/sample, builders -1,232,984 (-0.14%), http1-server -1,992 over 2,000 requests, typed +28 inside its copy gap; parseRanged +4.1% to +10.4% over parse
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: client side of the WebSocket opening handshake
entries.body:
nish/net/websocket now does both halves of the RFC 6455 opening handshake. A client calls websocketClientKey on 16 bytes from crypto.getRandomValues. websocketUpgradeRequest writes the GET upgrade request over nish/net/http1-client's request writer. websocketCheckResponse checks the 101, refusing each of RFC 6455 §4.1's client requirements with its own WS_HS_* code; a non-101 status stays readable. The bytes the parser kept after the head are the decoder's first input. A server can now choose a subprotocol from websocketOfferedProtocols.

nish/net/websocket still draws no randomness. The caller supplies the handshake nonce and every frame's mask, so the module stays sans-IO and keeps compiling to wasm32.

nish/net/http1-client gains an explicit per-request upgrade opt-in: http1UpgradeRequestHead, and Http1ResponseParser.expectUpgrade(), under which a 101 answers HTTP1_UPGRADE with tunnelBytes(). Without the opt-in, a Connection that lists upgrade and every 101 are still refused.

The loopback suite drops its hand-written GET and fixed key. It runs the client over plain TCP against Http1Server and over the std TLS client against Http1TlsServer, with random keys and masks, chat/superchat negotiation and a 1000 close. The response check gets a fuzz target with 18 seeds, recorded in docs/security/http1.md as not yet run under libFuzzer. The guide adds a /websocket page.

entries.title: record S3's decision and surface, and close the open WP38 housekeeping
entries.body:
WP38 records the owner's decision of 2026-10-30 (Q10) to build S3, nish:simd, on S3a's figures. §3.2 now gives the surface being built. u16x8 replaces i16x8, since Nish has no i16 scalar. There are four value-only mask types and an operation table. Conversions, shifts and saturating arithmetic are left for later. The Status line is current, and the CRC-32 kernel is part of it. S1b is recorded as superseded by S6c, which measured the same classifier as not reachable. #662's two acceptance criteria stand as shipped: the offset-index panic is native-only because Node does not check indexing, and a baseline capability report carries no cpu key. Earlier WP38 plan files now show which stages merged and which were cancelled, and pre-squash anchors name their PRs.

Refs: docs/wp38-simd.md#8-decisions
Closes #662

entries.title: run the Nish golden runner's slices in parallel itself
entries.body:
`build/nish-runner --jobs

` runs its `--shard` slice as `p` processes (one per core by default, at most 8), so CI's runner job no longer needs `scripts/nish-runner-parallel.mjs`, the Node wrapper that started one runner per core. The runner step is started under `env --default-signal`, because the Actions runner gives step shells an ignored SIGPIPE that Node used to reset. The `net_http_fetch` test proxy no longer closes an authorised CONNECT tunnel before reading the ClientHello, which had turned the close into a reset.

entries.title: JSON Pointer, value equality and exact decimals for JSON Schema
entries.body:
Three std modules a JSON Schema validator needs. nish/json-pointer parses, escapes and resolves RFC 6901 pointers over a JsonDocument, and checks pointer and relative-pointer syntax without allocating. nish/json-equal compares two values by JSON Schema's rules (1 equals 1.0, object members in any order) on an explicit stack, with a hash that agrees with it and a first-duplicate finder for uniqueItems. nish/json-number compares numbers and answers multipleOf exactly on their decimal text, never through f64, and refuses an exponent gap too wide to divide in bounded steps.

The const, enum, uniqueItems, multipleOf, minimum, maximum, exclusiveMinimum and exclusiveMaximum groups of JSON-Schema-Test-Suite draft2020-12 (MIT) are vendored under tests/json-schema-suite and pass.
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: the JSON Schema format checks
entries.body:
nish/json-format answers valid, invalid or unknown for each JSON Schema draft 2020-12 format it implements: date-time, date, time and duration (RFC 3339), email (RFC 5321 Mailbox), hostname, ipv4, ipv6, uuid, uri, uri-reference, iri, iri-reference, uri-template and regex. Every other format, json-pointer and the idn ones included, answers unknown.

Every check but regex is linear in its string, allocates nothing and cannot panic; regex compiles through nish/regex, so a pattern that needs lookaround or backreferences is a known false negative. The URI and IRI checks walk the RFC 3986/3987 grammar, because nish/net/url is deliberately stricter than the RFC.

The draft 2020-12 optional/format files of JSON-Schema-Test-Suite (MIT) are vendored under tests/json-schema-suite-format, and every string case of every implemented format gives the suite's answer.
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: load a YAML document into a JsonDocument with its source ranges
entries.body:
nish/yaml-json's YamlJsonLoader.load turns one document of a YamlStream into a JsonDocument, with every value's and key's range pointing at the YAML source, so one validator and one YamlLineIndex serve JSON and YAML alike. Scalars follow the YAML 1.2 core schema; hex and octal integers become exact decimal text; .inf and .nan, which JSON cannot hold, are refused with a code and the node's range. A failed load leaves the document as it was.

Aliases are expanded, and the expansion is sized before anything is built, so an alias bomb is refused at the alias against maxValues. Merge keys apply with the map's own keys winning, each map merged into a given map at most once, and every merge visit and merge-sequence walk is charged to a budget of maxValues plus the stream's node count, so a merge bomb is refused rather than run: a 60-level doubling chain that took 2^60 steps now loads in under a second. The parser's own merge check, in std/yaml.ts, still walks a shared merge sequence once per merge key; that is recorded open in docs/security/yaml.md.

std/yaml.ts is unchanged, and bench/yaml-compare runs the same code as main.
metrics: parse + load is 1.94x the parse in wall clock (2.27x in instructions) on a 1.1 MB OpenAPI document; the load step alone is 0.94x the parse (1.27x in instructions)
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: --sandbox confines a native program to main's capability set
entries.body: With --sandbox, a native program confines itself to the capability set the checker computes for main, before any of its code runs. A .preinit_array entry sets no_new_privs and drops capabilities. It applies Landlock to the fs rights main reaches and loads a seccomp denylist for the calls behind what it does not reach. A capability main does not reach is then withheld by the kernel, not only by the type checker, so neither FFI nor linked C can widen it. --sandbox=best-effort runs on where the kernel's Landlock is missing or too old, and says what it cannot withhold. darwin is refused with NL3044. Directory scopes are the next stage.
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: Unicode property escapes and case folding in nish/regex
entries.body:
regexCompile accepts the u flag, \p{…} and \P{…} (General_Category, Script, Script_Extensions and ECMA-262's binary properties, named as JavaScript names them, at Unicode 16.0.0), and Unicode simple case folding under i: σ matches Σ and ς, and classes are closed under folding. JSON Schema's pattern keyword is ECMA-262 with u, so schemas need all three. Lookaround and backreferences are still refused, so matching stays linear.

One deliberate difference from JavaScript: nothing folds across the ASCII boundary, so the Kelvin sign and ſ match no k or s. That keeps an ASCII pattern under i free of the tables. Patterns that use none of the new features compile to the same program as before.

The tables are generated from the UCD by scripts/gen-regex-unicode.mjs (--check verifies them against the UCD and Node's RegExp) and carry the Unicode License v3. They add 84,624 bytes to any program that imports nish/regex.
metrics: retired instructions a pass against main: literal, class, alternation, group, icase-ascii and icase-class 1.000x, anchored 0.992x, exec 0.926x; compiling a pattern that folds non-ASCII letters costs about 12 µs more for a large class and 0.2 µs for one é

entries.title: check a new type kind at every nesting depth
entries.body: .claude/architecture.md gains a rule for adding a type kind. Before review, try the kind nested at every depth a value can sit: a field, an array element, an inline array, a Result arm, a generic argument, a Map value, a parallel or task capture. entries.title: let a commit keep itself, or others, out of the changelog
entries.body:
changelog-gen turned every conventional commit in a release range into an
entry, so internal or unannounced work could not be kept out of the release
notes. Two trailers now do it: `Changelog: skip` drops the commit carrying it,
and `Changelog-Skip: <sha>[, <sha>...]` on any commit in the range drops the
named commits. Dropped commits never appear by subject, not even on stderr,
which prints only a count, and their type does not move the version. Two
internal entries are removed from the 0.27.0 record, and one sentence from a
0.22.0 entry.
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: keep P off bcrypt's critical path in the single-hash rounds
entries.body:
Each bcrypt half-round is x ^ P[n] ^ F(y), and only F(y) waits on the
previous half-round. LLVM's Reassociate and InstCombine put P[n] after
F(y) in 15 of 16 half-rounds, leaving two dependent XORs after the last
S-box add where gcc's build of the reference C has one. bcryptBody and
bcryptEncrypt now write each half-round as
ctSelect(0xffffffff, x ^ P[n], 0) ^ F(y): an identity on the value whose
all-ones mask sits behind the constant-time value barrier, so the XOR
with P cannot be folded into the chain and runs off the critical path.
Every hash and verify answer is unchanged, nothing secret-dependent is
added, and the wipes are as they were. The four-lane batch keeps the
plain form, where the barrier measured as a loss.
metrics: bcryptHash at cost 10, 73.1 (72.0-84.1) and 74.6 (72.1-76.9) ms on main against 67.8 (66.5-69.0) and 68.9 (66.6-71.0) ms, 7.3% and 7.6% faster, noise band about 2%; level with OpenBSD's gcc -O2 build

entries.body:

Two link programs hold both arms of the lowering to FIPS 180-4 digests,
RFC 4231 HMAC-SHA-256 tags and a seeded corpus hashed whole and in pieces;
the 'sha256 kernel' section links them with the kernel wrapped and proves
NISH_SHA256=soft leaves it unused, and that wasm32 builds reference none.

Tests: tests/link/sha256_hw_vectors, tests/link/sha256_hw_agree

* test(crypto): read the SHA-256 kernel's assembly for constant time

tests/ct-asm-runtime.js reads each runtime kernel unit with its resolver, so
runtime-sha256.c's nish_sha256_compress is held to the same model as the AES
kernels on x86-64, x86-64-v3 and aarch64.

* ci: run the SHA-256 kernel's paths on x86-64, AArch64 and Apple silicon

The x86-64 shard 1 requires the SHA-NI driver line and the lowered programs'
kernel calls; the AArch64 job runs the sha256 kernel section; the macOS job
holds the sysctl detection to the ARMv8 path and runs the SHA-256 link
programs under both pins. Each runner measures throughput per path once
bench/sha256 lands.

* fix(crypto): refuse a SHA-256 block past toI32's saturated length in the kernel

The kernel's guard read the source's real length, where sha256Compress's
reads it through toI32, which saturates at 2^31 - 1; a block ending past
that offset was refused by the walker and read by the kernel. The
aarch64 constant-time model also read sha256h, sha256h2, sha256su0 and
sha256su1 as overwriting their destination, which they accumulate into.

Tests: tests/simd/sha256.c, AUDIT_CORNERS in tests/ct-asm.js

* docs(crypto): record the SHA-256 block kernel's security review

The record says what runtime/runtime-sha256.c and its lowering were
checked for, how, and which test pins each property: SHA256HW-1, the
guard that read the source's length past toI32's saturation, fixed;
SHA256HW-2, the registers and spills no wipe reaches, open; and CT-20,
the aarch64 model's SHA-256 instructions, fixed. The guide, INSTALL.md
and std/README.md name NISH_SHA256, and the runtime is eleven units.

Refs: docs/security/crypto-sha256-hw.md

* docs(crypto): record the SHA-256 kernel's stage and figures in wp38-simd

Adds stage S8 to the SIMD plan: SHA-256's block function on SHA-NI and the
ARMv8 SHA-256 instructions, measured against the base and a byte-identical
copy of it, and why the SSSE3 and AVX2 message schedules for CPUs without
the instructions were not built.

Measured: x86-64 SHA-NI, 9 interleaved rounds, min: 1 MiB 228.5 to 1442.8 MB/s (6.31x), 1 KiB 5.72x, 64 B 2.37x, HS256 sign+verify 4520 to 1915 ns/op (2.36x); NISH_SHA256=soft within the base copy's band (<=4.7%)
Refs: docs/wp38-simd.md

* fix(crypto): count runtime-sha256.c among the runtime's eleven units

The --cpu check's unit regex skipped a file name with digits, so it never
counted runtime-sha256.c; it now counts all eleven. The comments, docs and
security records that still said ten now say eleven. The macOS SHA-256 step
allows only the `sha256 kernel` section's own Darwin SKIP lines, and requires

Tests: tests/run.js cpu-level, runtime cache

build.sh's wasm profile adds runtime-aes.c and runtime-sha256.c from one
loop over the kernels rather than two copies of it. tests/run.js reads

shellcheck SC2254: an unquoted expansion in a case pattern matches as a glob.

The line read "sha256 native arm64: sha256: N cases agree", which CI's
simd-arm64 grep for the armv8-sha2 path did not match.

* ci(crypto): run the SHA-256 checks on a macOS job of their own and compile runtime-sha256.c for darwin

The runtime-net job is disabled, so the Apple-silicon steps it carried never

path is compiled on every push. The throughput steps fail when a driver prints

as reading their destination.

Tests: tests/run.js (runtime-sha256 darwin), tests/ct-asm.js (AUDIT_CORNERS)

* docs(crypto): name sha256Compress's helpers as main has them in K1's scope

The sha256-macos job required a summary line of "N passed, 0 failed.", so

* docs: count thirteen runtime units wherever the runtime is counted

entries.title: measure syscall entry cost against TCP work per request
entries.body:
Add bench/syscall-cost: a C microbenchmark and its run script. They time a raw syscall's entry and exit (syscall(SYS_getppid)), recv with nothing queued, setsockopt(TCP_QUICKACK, 0), getsockopt(TCP_INFO), and a loopback request/response round at the bench server's bytes. Every figure is pinned to one CPU, reported as the median and min-max of interleaved rounds, and printed with the box's CPU, kernel and mitigation state. bench/README.md "Syscall cost" splits a keep-alive request's system time into (a) entry and exit and (b) the rest, for bench/http1-server.ts and as an estimate for a 3.6-syscall production mix. It records the verdict: on a Xeon @ 2.10 GHz VM on Linux 6.18 (eIBRS, no KPTI), entry and exit cost 106 ns. That is under the 0.5 µs line and about 4% of a request's 5 µs of system time, so io_uring is not worth building on this evidence. Run bench/syscall-cost/run.sh to re-measure on another box.

Measured: entry and exit 106.0 ns (101.9-113.2, 7 rounds of 10^6); (a) 0.22 µs of 4.89-5.51 µs sys per plaintext request, inside the h1/copy noise band of ~0.6 µs
Refs: bench/README.md#syscall-cost, docs/wp39-http-server.md
Part of #1084

entries.title: measure the cheaper ways to keep delayed ACKs
entries.body:
A keep-alive server that sets TCP_QUICKACK to 0 after every response, to keep delayed ACKs, pays one setsockopt per request for nothing. Linux keeps the delayed-ACK (pingpong) mode by itself. On 6.8 and 6.18 the tcp_pingpong_thresh sysctl defaults to 1, so tcp_event_data_sent enters pingpong on the first quick reply. Setting the option to 0 only enters that mode, and the mode is left only when a delayed-ACK timer fires. bench/quickack/README.md cites the kernel source by file and line. It tabulates each alternative: ip route quickack, TCP_CONGESTION, sysctls, BPF sockops, once at accept, no call, and a TCP_INFO check. It also gives the measured modes.

bench/http1-server.ts gains a BENCH_QUICKACK mode. Unset, the default, makes no call, as before. reset0, once0 and reset1 are the other modes. bench/http.mjs gains --acks, off by default, which reads the OutSegs and TcpExtDelayedACKs counters around each run. bench/quickack/probe.c measures the ACKs on one connection. The "Socket options" section of the networking guide now states the trade-off in both directions with the measured figures. No API is added. Setting the option once at accept, or not at all, needs only netSetOption. A TCP_INFO check would cost a getsockopt dearer than the setsockopt it replaces.

Measured: on a 4-vCPU Xeon @ 2.10 GHz VM on Linux 6.18 at c=256, reset1 costs +1.0 syscall and +1.000 segment per request and 12.9-18.3% fewer req/s, against a copy-vs-base noise band of -2.4% to +4.7%. reset0 adds +1.0 syscall per request and saves an ACK only after a slow response.
Refs: bench/quickack/README.md, docs/guide/using-nish/networking.md
Part of #1084

entries.title: add PgBatchClock, an adaptive batch timer for nish/net/postgres
entries.body:
A fixed batching window costs latency when traffic is quiet and buys nothing
near saturation. PgBatchClock decides when to start a batch from the times the
program passes in: once max(minCount, the moving average of recent batch sizes
times factor) items wait, once the oldest has waited maxWaitUs, or, with the
idle bypass on, at once when nothing is in flight and fewer than lightCount
items arrived in the last window. Under a backlog the count is already
waiting, so nothing waits on the timer and batches do not shrink. Its
average, last size, last wait and the reason each batch started (count,
average, timer, idle) are exposed for metrics.

PgBatcher.takeDue takes only when its clock says so, PgPool.inFlight gives the
clock its in-flight count, and PgBatchTurns lets one free connection collect
while the others execute, woken only once its batch is due. None reads a
clock or allocates per item. PgBatchClockConfig's defaults are the existing
fixed window; the adaptive settings are documented, and stay opt-in until a
live server's measurements say otherwise.

bench/pg-batch-clock.ts simulates a 4-connection pool at three steady rates
and compares fixed 10 ms and 30 ms windows with adaptive.
metrics: simulated, deterministic; adaptive p95 10.00/9.51/7.73 ms against the better fixed window's 10.00/9.62/7.74 ms at 5/42/84 % busy, server CPU per item within 2 % of the cheaper fixed window at 42 and 84 %

entries.title: bcrypt at any width from one to six lanes, and a calibrate that picks it
entries.body:
nish/crypto/bcrypt gains bcryptHashN and bcryptVerifyN, which hash or
verify one to six passwords interleaved on one core, and bcryptCalibrate,
which times every width at cost 4 on throwaway keys and returns the fastest
for the CPU it runs on. It measures rather than guesses and keeps nothing
between calls, so a service calls it once at startup. Every lane gives
bcryptHash's output byte for byte. bcryptHash4 and bcryptVerify4 keep their
signatures, outputs and errors and now run through the width-N path; the
single path is unchanged.

A single hash is one serial chain of 17,083,536 half-rounds, so it is bound
by latency: about 11 cycles per half-round, 173 cycles per Blowfish block,
level with libxcrypt's crypt_r. Lanes are the remaining lever. The security
record now gives cycles per block for the single path and per lane, the
latency floor and load-port bound, a verdict on each suspected overhead
(none of bounds checks, overflow checks, state reloads or wipes is in the
round loop), and why the kernel stays portable Nish rather than runtime C:
Nish's four lanes already match clang's four-lane C.

On a 4-core x86-64 Xeon at cost 10, the best width (four lanes) takes
22.2 ms per hash against 57.6 ms for bcryptHash and 59.0 ms for crypt_r.
AMD and AArch64 were not measured.
metrics: bcryptHashN 4 lanes 22.2 (21.9-25.2) ms/hash vs bcryptHash 57.6 (56.4-59.0), 2.6x throughput on one core; median and spread of 9 rounds, cost 10, 4-core x86-64 Xeon

entries.title: compression that pays for itself in nish/net/http-compress
entries.body:
HttpCompressor now sends gzip only when it is worth sending. Besides
minLength, minSaving and minSavingPercent refuse a body whose gzip saves
too few bytes or too small a share, and segmentMode sends gzip only when the
whole response, head included, needs fewer TCP segments of `mss` (the
connection's, or HTTP_DEFAULT_MSS, 1448) than it would as it is. Otherwise
the body goes as it is. `decision` reports why: SENT, NOT_ACCEPTED,
TOO_SMALL, TOO_LARGE, TOO_LITTLE_SAVED or NO_FEWER_SEGMENTS, so an
application can count them. Http1Connection.respondEncoded applies the
policy, withdrawing a gzip head with unrespond when segment mode decides
against it.

Bodies up to fixedLimit (16 KB) go through a new small-body encoder,
FixedDeflater / GzipFixedCompressor: one fixed-Huffman block, a 16 KB
window and no state kept between calls. On 0.5 to 16 KB of JSON it takes
0.22 to 0.44 times DEFLATE_FAST's time for about 1.35 times its bytes.
`encoder` picks it by size (HTTP_ENCODER_AUTO) or forces one encoder.

Vary: Accept-Encoding goes on every response whose form depended on the
request: a compressed one, or one sent as it is because gzip was not
accepted. A body that was too small, too large or did not pay is the same
for every client and carries none. identity;q=0 is honoured: such a request
gets gzip whatever the policy says. Compression stays off unless the
program asks for it, and nothing is cached between responses.

The MSS is configured, or set per connection (`conn.mss`). Reading it from
TCP_INFO or TCP_MAXSEG needs a nish:net builtin that does not exist yet.
metrics: fixed encoder 0.22-0.44x DEFLATE_FAST time at 1.33-1.38x its size, 560 B to 16 KB JSON, 9 rounds (bench/gzip/small.mjs)

50,000 responses of 0.5-8 KB JSON, MSS 1448, server CPU ±1 µs (10 ms ticks): none 19.0 µs, 2.44 segments; DEFLATE_FAST always 38.4 µs, 1.38 segments; fixed always 26.0 µs, 1.56 segments; segment mode 28.0 µs, 1.56 segments with 43% sent as is (bench/http-compress)
